utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hannis. I see that you're not alone this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning. We have a new face on our side this morning. To my right is Mr. Fergal Gaynor. Mr. Gaynor appears this morning because he wrote the Prosecution's response to the Defence motion, and in anticipation of dealing with that matter first, I've asked him to join me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we should start with dealing with that. I'm on page 5. I've not finished reading. I suggest ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest to the parties that we'll hear oral argument after we have heard the testimony of the 92 bis witnesses. Perhaps we should have informed you in advance in order to avoid that Mr. Gaynor shows up with high expectations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sure they will be met later on, Your Honour. And Ms. Karagiannakis is going to be calling the first witness, and she is in the booth. She'll be right in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we'll be ready for Mr. Dzafic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But there is one other issue we still have to deal with, and that is the exhibits that have been tendered through Witness 018. Madam Registrar, could you guide us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P30, under seal, the pseudonym sheet; and Exhibit P31, the decision on release from the Batkovic collection centre, dated 21 September 1992; and P31.1, the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since I did not hear any objections when they were presented to the witness, and since I do not see any objection or hear any objections at this moment, they are admitted into evidence. We then could give the opportunity to the Prosecution to call its next witness, which would be Mr. Dzafic, if I understood well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dzafic is a 92 bis witness from the Bratunac municipality. He was admitted, subject to cross-examination, by Your Honours' decision of 27th of January 2004, paragraph 8. There are three matters in relation to this witness, Your Honour, that we'd like to address. First, I'd like to read to Your Honours a summary of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Second, I'd like to confirm with the witness two clarifications that he has made to his 92 bis statement dated the 20th of June, 2000, after he arrived in The Hague. And finally, Your Honours, I'd like to tender one exhibit that was parted of the witness's 92 bis testimony in Milosevic and ask him a couple of brief questions about that one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because we are not only dealing with the 92 bis statements but also with the transcript of his testimony given in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps for your information in general, if a request is made to receive in evidence a transcript of the testimony of a witness does not automatically include all the exhibits that were referred to during the testimony. So they have to be tendered additionally. They're usually also not attached to the transcript. And the Chamber would like to ask the parties to tender those exhibits that are of great relevance. Sometimes even if a witness is testifying and if exhibits are tendered, it's not always necessary to understand their testimony without, if not all, then some of these exhibits. On the other hand, there may well be exhibits that are of great importance to the testimony and it goes without saying that the Chamber under these circumstances would very much like to have these exhibits tendered into evidence as well. But that's approximately what the Chamber would like to receive. These were the -- you told us about the summary, about additional questions, and about the exhibits. Yes. That's it. Then, Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Dzafic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dzafic, I think you are. Before giving evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration. The text of that solemn declaration will be handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated. It appears to me that the witness could hear me in a language he understands. Mr. Krajisnik, I take it, since I didn't hear from you, that the same is true from you. Yes. I see that you are confirming this by nodding. Mr. Dzafic, you'll first be examined by the Prosecution, but since you've given already a statement, and since the Chamber and the parties have read that statement, there will be a short summary of your statement, then some additional questions, perhaps also in respect of the testimony you've given earlier in this Court will be put to you, but most of the questions then will be put to you by Defence counsel. Ms. Karagiannakis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The following is a summary of the witness's evidence. Suad Dzafic is from near Vitkovici, Bratunac municipality. He explains that when he returned from Serbia to his home village -- he explains that he returned from Serbia to his home village in Bratunac municipality in March 1992. He describes firsthand knowledge of the fate of both himself and his fellow villagers. His statement also covers his hearsay knowledge of the takeover of Bratunac town and other Muslim villages in the Bratunac municipality in April and May of 1992. The witness attests that Krasan Polje, a neighbouring village, was attacked on the 10th of May, 1992. The same day, Serb neighbours came and told the witness and his fellow villagers that they would be safer if they fled into the woods. They did flee to the forest but returned the same night. From the 10th to the 18th of May, 1992, Serb police patrolled the village. On the 17th of May, 1992, the chief of police came and asked them to hand in any weapons they owned. On the morning of 18 May 1992, their Serb neighbours who were armed and in camouflage uniforms surrounded the village. Suad Dzafic, along with his fellow villagers, were then put onto buses and transferred to Bratunac. Around 3.00 p.m., the buses left Bratunac and travelled on to Vlasenica. Each bus had an armed guard on board. When they arrived in Vlasenica, they parked near the bus station. The buses were surrounded by a mixed group of soldiers. Suad Dzafic identified some of these guards as being Arkan's Tigers and others as Beli Orlovi. 34 military age men and also five minors were taken to the Vlasenica MUP or SUP prison by soldiers. Two men were taken out of the group. 32 military-aged men and minors were detained there until the 21st of May, 1992. During this time, they were beaten and maltreated by Serb soldiers. On 21st May 1992, the military-aged men were ordered out of the Vlasenica by two policemen and put on a bus. Soldiers then asked the detainees to hand over personal belongings, including money and documents. An armoured vehicle was parked near the bus and four cars also joined the bus. One of these cars had a skull on its doors. Together the vehicles formed a convoy which left Vlasenica in the direction of Bratunac. The convoy stopped in a cafe for about 30 minutes. It continued on in the direction of Bratunac. The convoy then stopped at the entrance of the village of Nova Kasaba and the men were ordered off the bus in groups of about five. As they left the bus they were shot by soldiers using automatic rifles and the machine-gun mounted on the armoured vehicle. Suad Dzafic was in the last group to get off the bus with his brother, two cousins and another male relative. As they stepped out they were hit by gunfire. The witness was hit from both automatic rifles and heavy machine gunfire. He fell to the ground but survived. The witness identified two soldiers who participated in this mass execution, an individual called Makedonac and Pero Mitrovic who had been a neighbour of his in Vitkovici. Immediately after the execution these two individuals looked for and shot the survivors. Suad Dzafic ultimately managed to flee the execution site and reached Muslim-held territory. Your Honours, that concludes the summary. I now have a couple of additional questions. If the witness could be shown his 92 bis declaration in B/C/S and the parties could refer to the English translation of the statement which is attached and dated 20 June 2000. And for ease of reference, I've numbered the paragraphs on the English version. Examined by Ms. Karagiannakis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please confirm that when you came to The Hague, you had an opportunity to review the statement in front of you now.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please refer to paragraph 30 of that statement. Have a look at paragraph 30. It's the third paragraph on page 5 of the English version. Mr. Dzafic, can you please confirm that in relation to paragraph 30, the sentence beginning "at some point," that that sentence and the following sentences in that paragraph should be deleted and replaced with the phrase "at some point, soldiers requested us to hand over all our personal belongings, including money and documents. We did so." Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Secondly, can I ask you to look at paragraph 43 of your statement. Can you -- in relation to paragraph 43, can you please confirm that this sentence should be replaced by the sentence: "I was in the last group along with my brother, two cousins, and another male relative. My father had been taken out in a group before me. As we stepped out, we were hit by gunfire." Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Now, can the witness please be shown the following exhibit, which is a list. Your Honours, I should explain what this exhibit is. As you know, the witness testified in the Milosevic trial, and the relevant parts of the transcript of his testimony was included in the 92 bis package. Milosevic Exhibit 473, titled "List of those killed on 21 May 1992 near Nova Kasaba, Vlasenica municipality, drawn up by Suad Dzafic" was tendered through this witness in his testimony at transcript page number 23212. Your Honours, we seek to have this exhibit given an exhibit number in this case and admitted into evidence, and then I'd like to ask the -- I'd like to ask the witness a couple of questions in relation to the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This list will be Prosecution Exhibit number P32.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzafic, does this list in front of you represent the names of people that were related to you or that you knew by name who were shot on the 21st of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the list. That is the list, but it's not the final list. There were other people there. I drew up this list and included the cousins and the relatives and my neighbours whom I recalled at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the ethnicity of the people on that list?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That concludes my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Karagiannakis. Is the Defence ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed, Ms. Loukas. Cross-examined by Ms. Loukas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzafic -- Mr. Dzafic, it would help if you looked at me. I'm over here. Now, Mr. Dzafic, if I say something you don't understand or you need time to compose yourself, just let me know. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to your statement, Mr. Dzafic, I think you gave a statement on 20th of June, 2000. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I propose to show the witness the statement and refer to various paragraphs. So I'm just -- there's a copy of the English statement and a copy of the B/C/S statement. I can indicate that the paragraphs are numbered. I would also indicate to Your Honour: Unfortunately, I don't have any further copies this morning for the interpreters and the rest of the Court, because, despite equality of arms, the photocopier in the Defence room wasn't working last night or this morning. But nevertheless, I forwarded this to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whenever then comes to reading, would you please do it slowly so that the interpreters --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I will do it very slowly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. Sorry. I understand that this is exactly what I've previously tendered to Your Honours, the statement numbered English version, so perhaps for ease of reference, I think it's already been distributed to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the interpreters -- it's the 20th of June statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It's the 20th of June statement, Your Honour. So if that's already been distributed by the Prosecution, that's more than adequate. But I can -- but does he have a numbered B/C/S version? They're both numbered?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Perhaps we -- I can confirm that I think the numbered paragraphs conclude with the number 60 on the statement dated -- number 60, dated the 20th of June. So if your statement concludes number 60 as well then --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I think the registry is just checking that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. From what I see, we have numbered version of both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It's just to ensure that they're numbered in exactly the same way. But I think the registry now confirms that. I see some nodding. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzafic, you have the statements before you in both English and B/C/S; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as I mentioned previously, you gave a statement on the 20th of June of the year 2000; correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you subsequently gave a further corrections statement. Now, that statement appears to be undated. Do you remember when you gave that corrections statement?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you gave a further corrections statement on the 10th of February, is that correct, of this year?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course you've previously given evidence at this Tribunal on the 26th and the 27th of June, 2003, last year?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, going to your statement, at paragraph 4 -- have you got paragraph 4 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicate there in paragraph 4 that you'd heard that some Muslim people had been killed by the Bosnian Serb. Do you see that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that here. But that's where I made the correction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that you made that second, subsequent correction in relation to that. Yes. Now, but what I want to confirm there in relation to paragraph 4 is that this was just information that you'd heard. It obviously wasn't firsthand information. That's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No, that's something I heard. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when we come to paragraph 5, and I think you'd also made a correction in that paragraph as well. Just confirm that. In any event, in relation to paragraph 5, again you say you indicate that you'd -- at the very beginning of April "I heard ..." And then you go on to recite information there. Again, paragraph 5 is information that you'd heard about; it's not firsthand information. That's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's the same for paragraph 6?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Ask me a question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That is the same in relation to paragraph 6, that is, that this is information you'd heard about, not information that you'd personally observed, Mr. Dzafic?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same in relation to paragraph 7, again, that is information that you heard, not information from firsthand knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again in relation to paragraph 8, that is information you'd heard from others, not information that you'd acquired personally; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I heard. I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also paragraph 9 and 10, the same situation, information that you heard rather than information that you in any way personally witnessed. That's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 9, I saw that in my village, because the local Serbs joined the paramilitary units and they established this Serb army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So paragraph 9, you say there's some personal knowledge there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, personal knowledge. It's something that I saw and heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's a combination of seeing that and hearing about it as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It's a combination, because the people, my Serb neighbours, they're also from the municipality of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, paragraph 10, that's information that is -- you've heard from other people; that's not information that you have personal knowledge about?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I have to read paragraph 10, because I don't know this off by heart. I have to see what it's about, and then I can say whether it's something I had seen or just heard of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I invite you, Mr. Dzafic, to read paragraph 10.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. I've read it. This is something that I heard about and it's also something that I saw. Everything that it says in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So which bits did you see?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I saw them attacking the village next to mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That village, are you referring to Krasan Polje?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that village is two kilometres away from your village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you'd agree you weren't exactly seeing it up close?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. In fact, what I think -- I think you indicated in your statement you can see from two kilometres away, you could see houses burning; is that correct? And hear shootings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you saw from two kilometres away houses burning and heard some shootings; right? So that's --

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- the extent of what you can rely on your personal knowledge for in paragraph 10; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: That's what I saw. I saw that with my own eyes. I saw the houses burning and I heard shooting. I heard about the rest of the villages around Bratunac. But this village, Krasan Polje, I saw that personally with my own eyes as the houses were burning, and I saw the shooting. In my house in the evening, Golub Djurkovic came. He was wearing a uniform. He was wearing the uniform of a Serb police officer. It was a multicoloured uniform. And he told us that he took part in the attack on Krasan Polje that day, and he also named the people who were killed. That is not in the statement, but that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzafic, just getting back to my question, and it would really help if you answered my questions, as opposed to going off into other areas. Because if there's anything that needs to be cleared up, the Prosecutor will do that in re-examination. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I understand that. Please ask me a question and I will reply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, getting back to paragraph 10, so the extent of your personal knowledge in relation to paragraph 10 is that you saw from two kilometres away houses burning and heard shootings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And obviously, you'd agree with me you couldn't see a lot more than that from two kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't tell the people apart, but I could see a lot of what was going on there, and I did see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as you've indicated, obviously you couldn't tell the people apart; agreed?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. But with the confirmation of this man who took part in this himself, I found out who else took part in this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that. But again, Mr. Dzafic, we have to be able to determine what is your own personal knowledge and what is information you've just heard from other people. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, if the witness explains and if you make a clear distinction between firsthand knowledge and what is hearsay, if the witness would like to explain his position, he should be entitled to do so. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzafic, paragraph 11, that's also information you've just heard about and not information that you personally witnessed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the village of Glogova. This is something that I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in relation to these various aspects that you cover in paragraphs 4 to 11 of your statement, the things you heard from other people, do you remember who these people were?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: That I heard that from. I don't remember. I mentioned a little bit earlier one person whom I heard some things from. Then I also heard from my father about one man from Bratunac who was killed. His name was Sulco.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So you've nominated earlier in your evidence a person that you heard something from in relation to these paragraphs 4 to 11, and you've also nominated something that your father said to you.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. My father told me that this Sulco was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. But you don't remember the other people who they were that you heard things from, other than these two people you've nominated: Your father and this other man. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't remember the people who told me about these things that we have covered so far.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzafic, if I could just take you to paragraph 28 of your statement. Have you got that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, I'm going to ask you some questions about paragraph 28, so if you'd like to take some minutes to read it prior to my asking you the questions. Okay?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've read that now, Mr. Dzafic?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated there in that particular paragraph that: "On the morning of the 21st, a Serb in camouflage uniform came to the cell and told us that we would have survived for one more day, we would have been safe."

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what was the purpose of that particular man's visit to the cell?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I can explain to you now what his intention was. He came in uniform. He didn't have a weapon on him. He opened the door to our cell and he stood inside the door, and he was talking to us. And he said: "If you survive one more day, you will most probably be safe. Because those people who are supposed to do all the killings, they are paid up to the 31st of May, or up to June, and they will be withdrawing from the field."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You've indicated that in your statement, and you've indicated there that this particular soldier gave you that information. Now, so basically your evidence there is that a man you didn't know -- is that correct? You'd never met him before, this man?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this man, a man you've never met before, a Serb in camouflage uniform, comes up and gives you that information; is that correct? That's your evidence?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he basically turns up out of nowhere to announce this important information to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't know where he came from. He just came to this door, and he was standing inside the open door and he was talking to us, but I don't know where he had come from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had never seen him before and he gave you this information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No, I had never seen him before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then in that same paragraph, Mr. Dzafic, you indicate that: "I already knew, as I was told by some other Serb soldiers, that those paramilitary units had been hired by SDS leadership members of Bratunac, with the precise duty to kill as many Muslims as they can." Do you see that sentence in your paragraph 28?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who were these other Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't know them either; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these other Serb soldiers that you've referred to there, when did they convey that information to you?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember, but they told us that day. This was 12 or 13 years ago, so I cannot really remember such things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you cannot remember when in relation to the events that information was given to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, I remember that day, the 21st of May, that same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it possible for you to recollect now whether it was a matter of hours or a matter of days when these other Serb soldiers who you don't know gave you that information?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The witness has already said on two occasions that he was given that information on that same day, and the question was: Was it a matter of hours or days from when he was first provided with the information.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to that, he hasn't indicated that. If one checks the transcript. He said he didn't remember when that information had been received, as I read the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Line 19 reads: "Well, I remember that day, the 21st of May, that same day."

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, he says he remembers that day, but I don't think his answer implied that that was the day he received that second lot of information from unknown soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That same day you understand it that way. You could understand it in two different ways. Just to better understand your testimony at this moment, the information you got from the other soldiers, did you -- was your testimony that you received that on that same day or could it have been the day before or two days before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All on the same day. I received the information on the 21st of May, the same day that soldier told us if we survived one more day, we will be saved, we will survive. I received that other information on the same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on this day, the 21st of May, a Serb in camouflage uniform comes to the cell and provides that information about you'll survive for one -- if you survive for one more day, you'll be all right. I'm paraphrasing here. Because the people responsible for the killings in Bratunac are about to leave and they've only been paid until the end of May. Right? So that's the first bit of information you get from an unknown Serb, is that correct, on the 21st of May?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you say that you were told on the same day, by some other unknown Serbs, that those paramilitary units had been hired by SDS leadership members of Bratunac, with the precise duty to kill as many Muslims as they can. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So on the 21st of May, you receive this information and both from people you don't know -- I think that basically summarises the position. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I got the information from people that I don't know. I don't know them by name. These were people in uniforms. The uniform was the uniform of the Serb police and military. There were all kinds of uniforms there. These were not people in civilian clothing who came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, these people who you say gave you the information about the duty to kill as many Muslims as they can, what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Multicoloured uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of colours?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Green and ... Camouflage uniforms. They were multicoloured. They had green on it and ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these people that told you these things were men in camouflage uniforms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all the people that told you the things that you've got in your paragraph 28 were all unknown Serbs in camouflage uniform; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzafic, just in relation to your statement that you gave on the 20th of June, and of course it is the situation that you've given two subsequent correction statements as well, but I just want to take you specifically now to your statement of 20th of June. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when your statement was taken, Mr. Dzafic, there was, of course, somebody there taking notes?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, you might have to move closer to the microphone, because when you say "da," and you're a little further from the microphone, the interpreter can't hear it and it doesn't come back through the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, you could perhaps adjust the direction of the microphones a bit. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzafic, when that statement was taken, of course you appreciated that the Prosecution needed your testimony to investigate the things that had happened to you; that's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course to find the people responsible; that's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course that they needed your signature on that statement to prosecute the people who had done these terrible things to you?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course, after what had happened to you, you knew how important it was to tell the truth; that's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that now was the time to tell the truth; that's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, the truth would have been burning inside you; that's correct, is it not, Mr. Dzafic?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain what you mean when you say "burning inside me"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you lost some very important people in your life, did you not, Mr. Dzafic?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. I lost two brothers, my father, and other relatives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what I'm putting to you is that, in view of all that had happened, that the truth would have been burning inside you and you would want to tell the Prosecution the truth about everything that happened. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you wanted to tell them the truth about everything you knew?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. What I saw and what I went through also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course, you gave a very detailed statement. You gave a very detailed statement, Mr. Dzafic; that's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Do you mean did I say everything that I wanted to say? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'm asking you if you consider your statement to be detailed.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many hours did it take to conduct the interview?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember if it took a whole day or half a day?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, it was finished, more or less, in one day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzafic, the interviewers, of course, were very careful with you in writing down what you had to say; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, what about coming to your point. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, Mr. Dzafic, you had a chance to read the entire statement before you signed it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you signed that statement, you were asked whether everything was true?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were asked whether there was anything you could add; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzafic, going to paragraph 4 in your statement. Now, Mr. Dzafic, I realise that you've subsequently corrected this in another statement, but what's stated there, is it not, is that: "In March 1992, I heard that some Muslim people had been killed by the Bosnian Serb in Bascarsija, Sarajevo." Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I can see that. But that's where I made a correction. A killing happened, but who killed who, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And I think you actually gave evidence of that in the trial against Mr. Milosevic. That's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said: "Well, I don't know who killed who. I just heard that a killing had taken place." You'd agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So even though you didn't know who killed who, you put in your statement that you'd heard some Muslim people had been killed by Bosnian Serb. That's the situation, is it not, Mr. Dzafic?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says in this statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's in fact wrong, Mr. Dzafic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is not correct. It's inaccurate, and I made a correction. I was not sure at first. I knew that the killing happened, but who killed who, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But even though you didn't know who killed who, what you put in your statement was that it was Muslim people that had been killed by Bosnian Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said, but then I corrected it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that. But all I'm saying is what appears in your statement is what appears in your statement, Mr. Dzafic. You'd agree with that; yes?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. But even if you take a statement ten times, ten times you will not be able to take the same statement. It's not a song that you learn by heart and then recite it. It's not a poem. It's an experience that you cannot describe every time the same way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you don't know something, Mr. Dzafic, you just assume that it's Muslim people being killed by Bosnian Serbs, do you?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it says in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, it took you quite some time to come to your point, and now your problem is to get away from your point again. You made your point.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I wasn't going to go any further on that particular point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But perhaps next time halfway would be sufficient for a non-lay Bench.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I understand that Your Honour would prefer me to do it faster and not in the jury manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It was perfectly clear, I would say, after one or two questions, it was already clear from what we read in the Milosevic testimony, that the statement of the witness in this respect was incorrect, and what -- I think the point you'd like to make is that if someone hears about an event, he interprets that event according to what he expects, perhaps, it has been, and that was clear already after the first one or two questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, taking you now to paragraph 25 and 26, Mr. Dzafic. Do you have those paragraphs before you?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there you indicate -- would you like an opportunity to quickly read those paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just to confirm what you're saying there, you're saying that there were 32 of you locked in a cell of 3 by 5 metres; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. 32 plus five minors. That's a total of 37.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So -- and you've indicated there that in this room of 32 plus five minors, you were beaten by five Serb soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzafic, that's an exaggeration, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: What's an exaggeration?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That in a room of 3 metres by 5 metres, 32 men plus 5 minors were beaten by 5 Serbs.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Oh, yes, that's possible. Everything's possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzafic, of course everything's possible, but this Tribunal is trying to find the truth. Now, Mr. Dzafic --

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: That is the truth. What I said is the truth. The room was approximately 3 by 5 metres. We were 37. Five soldiers came to beat us. Half of the room was empty when they came to beat us. That means that 37 of us fit into only half the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just in relation to your paragraph 28, if you would just have a look at that, paragraph 28 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. We've been through this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: And we described it the way it was. Do you want me to repeat it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I don't. You'd better wait for the question. Mr. Dzafic, paragraph 28 is also an exaggeration, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No. No, certainly not. That's something I lived through and survived.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Loukas. Is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Just a few brief questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. Re-examined by Ms. Karagiannakis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you please look at paragraph 5 of your statement. From what source did you hear of -- hear about the takeover of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I heard reports on television, and the only television we could receive in my village was TV Belgrade. So I heard from the media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In relation to paragraphs 6 and 7, I think you mentioned in relation to those that your father told you about the murder of one Sulco. Can you tell us what your father -- where your father was working -- can you tell us where your father was working in April and May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: He wasn't working at all in May. In the beginning of April, he did work, in the factory called 9th October, in Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which town was that factory?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was it Bratunac town in Bratunac municipality or was it some other town?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, it's far from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: It's two kilometres away from the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And what did he tell you about the death of Sulco?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: He didn't see this killing. He heard from others that Sulco was taken away and detained, arrested, and taken to the Drina River and killed. So he passed on to me the information that he had from others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you look at paragraph 8, what's the source of your information for people being detained at the Vuk Karadzic Primary School?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: You mean from whom I heard this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: From people. I heard people saying that some people from villages were taken to the football field. A part of them were taken to the Vuk Karadzic School. And I heard this from people who survived the detention in the Vuk Karadzic School.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in relation to paragraph 10, if you have a look at paragraph 10.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of view did you have from your village to the village of Krasan Polje?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I had a good view. It was about two kilometres away. My village was slightly higher, and this lay in a clearing, no obstacles, and you could see everything. You could see people walking. That's the kind of view I had. It was a good vantage point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in relation to your evidence regarding paragraph 10, you said you couldn't tell the people apart. Now, -- and you just said you were able to see people. Were you able to see what people were wearing?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No. That I could not see. I was able to see people, but I could not distinguish who they were. I could not tell who they were, nor could I tell how they were dressed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned being told about takeovers from Golub Djurkovic. Could you tell us who he is?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you know him before the war?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was a neighbour of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: On that day, the 10th of May, in the evening, he came to see us, along with a couple of other neighbours. We were sitting and talking over drinks. He told us what was going on in Krasan Polje and he started saying that in Krasan Polje, people were expelled, some of them were killed. We asked why, and he replied: "They were nationalists, they had weapons in their possession."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know what the -- did you know or did he tell you what the ethnicity of the people that were killed and expelled were?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: They were of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Karagiannakis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got one question for you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've told us that you got information from others about the people who were supposed to kill as much as they could and that you received that information on that same day. Were you told this when you were in this cell together with others, or was it outside the cell? What were the circumstances under which you received that information?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: We were inside the cell. People would open the door of the cell and stand in the doorway, between the cell, that is, and the hallway. And standing in the doorway, they would start a conversation. And on one occasion, they told us that those were the orders. Because this was happening in the neighbouring municipality, Vlasenica, and those people were probably from Vlasenica. And they told us: Your people from Bratunac municipality ordered that as many Muslims as possible should be killed and that should be done by the group who was in charge of this and paid to do this. And this should be done by the beginning of June, and then they would withdraw. And they were probably talking about paramilitary units. Because at my own execution, what I saw at my own execution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: What I saw at my own execution were those soldiers who wore the insignia of White Eagles. I also noticed markings on a vehicle, skulls and the writing "White Eagles," as well "Arkan's men," and there are also Tigers. I saw such insignia on one sabotage platoon. A man I knew was also a member of the police in Belgrade. And when we saw him, we were happy. We thought we would be exchanged or released. Because he had spent so many vacations together with us in our village, which was his home village. He was born there, and he moved as a young man to Sabac, in Serbia. That's where he probably finished school and worked in Belgrade as a policeman. His name was Pero Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me stop you here, not because it might not be interesting to hear, but I think you could go on telling us about what happened for many hours. I was mainly interested to hear about under what circumstances you got the information from the other people. Did there ever come to your cell anyone who you did not regard as someone who was in charge of keeping you in detention, outsiders?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't quite understand your question. You mean did somebody come from outside who would not do a thing like that, who would not keep us in prison?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Who was not involved in keeping you in prison.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I didn't know those people, and I did not see them at the execution. Those people who came were not carrying weapons, and there were other people who were beating us. I cannot know who the people were who were not ... I cannot know their intentions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're not quite sure about the specific position and function of those people who came to your cell.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: The people who told us this ... People would come in. One set of people would come in to beat us. There were two men whom I didn't know but whom I remembered, and I later knew -- found out their names. The other people would just stand in the doorway and, through a conversation, they related to us this piece of information. If you mean some people who held positions in the municipality, I don't know whether those people held positions in the municipality or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I've not been clear enough. Did you consider those people who came to you and had these conversations with you all to belong to the group, unit, whatever you call it, that was in charge of keeping you in detention?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't know to which units they belonged, but they were wearing uniforms. I can't see what's going on in their minds. I don't know whether they were in charge of keeping us detained. I couldn't read their minds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers. Mr. Dzafic, unless the -- one of the parties would have any question in relation to questions by the Bench --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This concludes your testimony in this Court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming and giving answers to questions of both parties and of the Bench, and I hope that you have a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we are at five minutes -- 25 minutes past 10.00. I'd first like to deal with the exhibits shown to this witness. I do understand on your list there are also some non-exhibits, which is ... So I will disregard them. On the other hand, there might be some problem if these statements are not exhibits. If it would ever come to a hearing in the Appeals Chamber, then of course all the reference to paragraphs is not the most easy one. We will consider how to find a solution for that. Perhaps if the parties would agree that 92 bis statements could be provided with paragraph numbering, which really facilitates the examination of the witnesses, then we should find a way of introducing these paragraph numbers. But how technically to do it, because they have been tendered already -- they have been submitted already. Decisions are taken already in respect of their admission. On the other hand, I do not know whether --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, just in this instance, I think the best approach would be for the exhibits to be tendered by the Defence, with the numbered paragraphs, in light of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would be a solution. But it doubles, approximately, the amount of paper, and as one of my former colleagues always said, it saves half a forest if you stop copying halfway. We'll consider how to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: In terms of future arrangements for 92 bis witnesses, Your Honour, I think it would be very useful to have the numbered paragraphs from here on in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As long as it is clear what has been added in a later stage, and what was original in the 92 bis statement, and if the parties would agree on that, it would certainly help.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I understand that the Rule 92 bis actually requires that in the B/C/S version is numbered, so the issue then becomes the numbering, the appropriate numbering of the English translation, but as Your Honour said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll find a solution for that. But at this moment, Madam Registrar, could you guide us through the, not the non-exhibits, but the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There is one exhibit, Exhibit P32 is the list of witnesses -- sorry, the list of persons killed on 21 May 1992, compiled by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I've heard no objections. Therefore, P32 is admitted into evidence. It's of no use to call the next witness. We'll adjourn until 10 minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make a couple of comments before we do. One, Your Honour, I must say, although it's water under the bridge, I'm coming fairly new to this Tribunal, it's with absolute amazement that we realise all the years this Tribunal has been in operation it never seems to have occurred to anybody that it might be helpful actually to have the 92 bis statements or the potential 92 bis statements prepared with paragraph numbering in the first place. But given that apparently over many, many years hasn't occurred to anybody, we wonder whether it is possible simply to have some of them -- to have the numbering done on a word processor rather than everybody have to keep adding numbering. Apparently, according to my learned friend in the B/C/S version it's done, so there's hardly an issue about the numbering because it's going to match the B/C/S versions. But it's a technical matter, but certainly we entirely endorse Your Honour's comments that anything that prevents the need for even more extensive photocopying would be extremely welcome. My second comment is only this, intended to be helpful to the Tribunal, as indeed was that one, which is that in case Your Honours are spending time on the motion, I have made clear to the Prosecution this morning that we are - in the light of the response, we've considered the matter carefully overnight - we are no longer going to press for the evidence of Mr. Deronjic to be completely excluded. Our submissions on this matter are going to be in relation to the timing of his evidence in relation to his imminent sentencing, and I've made that clear to Mr. Hannis before the Tribunal sat this morning. So I didn't want Your Honour and Your Honour's colleagues to spend any time on an unnecessary issue. The third point is this, Your Honour: That there is in relation to the next witness, Mr. Dubicic, there is some further ground which is proposed by the Prosecution to be covered, since he has arrived in The Hague to give evidence, the Prosecution have obtained some further information from him which has been given to us in the form of an addendum. I'm not quite sure what's being handed up at the moment to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is handed up is -- at least it appears on the list as being two non-exhibits, and it might relate to what you're addressing at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I think not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Supplementary information sheet dated the 10th of February 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the other one is the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour it would be more appropriate if that information were not handed to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I only have looked at the front page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... That's why I asked the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Because the very next page, the next two pages are precisely that information and it would, although Your Honours are not a jury and of course have that worldwide judicial ability to exclude from your minds material which has been received into your mind, it's still better for Your Honours not to receive the information in the first place if that can be managed. The -- but the practical point is this, Your Honour: That without going into it at all, it does require me to have an opportunity to discuss with Mr. Krajisnik this matter. Therefore, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Usually an arrangement can be made during the breaks to meet with Mr. Krajisnik. So if that would enable you to at least to clarify your own position. I do understand that if new issues are suggested on such short notice, that the Defence should have time to prepare for it. Since I do not know what it is about, apart from that it's supplemental information, I haven't looked any further, I invite you to see whether and to seek the assistance to meet with Mr. Krajisnik during the break, and then see how we proceed after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, simply going to ask if we could at this stage, could we possibly have an additional ten minutes and that would enable me as a preliminary matter just to see what's needed because it may or may not take a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises for being back later than announced. In respect of the next witness, I still haven't opened it, Mr. Stewart. Perhaps we should first hear from the Prosecution what makes it so urgent to add anything to the subject matter of the testimony. But before inviting you to do so, is my recollection correct that the Prosecution opposed against calling this witness for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please explain to us, also perhaps in view of your answer to the last question, what makes it so important to add to the subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. When this witness arrived earlier in the week, in sitting with him to proof him for his testimony before you, he indicated that he had some information, particularly regarding this accused, that he had had some personal dealings with him, a couple of phone conversations and a meeting. None of that was in his prior statement, that was something that we were unaware of. That seemed to be information that was particularly pertinent to this case. After finishing talking with him, we typed that up in the statement that you haven't looked at yet but that we sent to Defence counsel last night. It seems to be something that is in the nature of the way we have investigated and prosecuted case here. A statement sometimes was taken, I think in this case, it was 1999, but we have statements from some witnesses that were taken in 1995 and 1996, when the focus of the investigation was just trying to get a rough idea of what had happened, as opposed to focussing on a particular individual accused. In this case, we proposed this witness's statement as a 92 bis statement because he had general information about the municipality of Bratunac and certain events that had occurred there, but there was nothing in his statement about his knowledge of or his dealings with this particular accused. When he was here, it just seemed like something that I would be -- or any representative from my office would be derelict in our duty if we didn't at least inquire whether or not he had any personal knowledge about this accused or any dealings with him. And in the course of doing that, that's when we learned this information. We feel it's pertinent and we propose it. If the Defence needs more time in light of the late revelation of this, we certainly can't disagree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, what is the position of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's this, Your Honour: We say that this addition should not be allowed to the evidence. We can understand completely the practical reasons why initially when the statement was taken it did not focus specifically on Mr. Krajisnik. We understand that. This one was 1999, but of course that was the year before Mr. Krajisnik was arrested, whatever the position might have been thought to be as far as Mr. Krajisnik's future was concerned. But the -- but it's not as if the arrival of the witness in The Hague is the only opportunity to raise what, in the light of Mr. Krajisnik's indictment nearly four years ago now, is a very obvious question to raise: Has there been any contact or communication between you, Witness, and Mr. Krajisnik? After all, there is contact with the witness. Otherwise it would be impossible to actually get him here to The Hague. And it's a very simple inquiry to make in writing. In the first place, the inquiry can simply be: Has there any been contact or was they any contact or communication between you and Mr. Krajisnik? If the answer is no, then it's the end of the question. If the answer is yes, and it's important, then it can be followed up in good time. So while clearly the aim of this Tribunal is not to unnecessarily punish or penalise parties for any oversights in the preparation of a case, there are limits, and it is really entirely different aspect of evidence to bring in direct contact with the accused. Now, I'm not saying it's in principle unmanageable, because of course it isn't, Your Honour. We could, given time, handle the matter. We would need time to do that. I do make that clear and the Prosecution acknowledge it. But we do say, and of course Your Honour's question is pertinent as well. After all, in a sense, it's only accidental, as far as the Prosecution is concerned, that this opportunity to ask this question of this particular witness has arisen at all. They didn't want him to come to The Hague at all. It's only because we wished to cross-examine him that he's got here. I don't criticise him for asking the question at this stage given that they haven't asked it before. That's not the point. Of course, as Mr. Hannis correctly says, better late than never, as I paraphrase what he's saying. Dereliction of duty if they didn't ask it at this very late stage. But it is, we say, too late, and it is inappropriate in this particular case that this significant addition. By way of contact with Mr. Krajisnik, not alluded to in the previous statements at all should be allowed. Your Honour, the point is a short one. There's really no more to say than that, except that yes, if we were to have to deal with this, then we would need more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And just to be very practical and not preluding on any decisions as the Chamber has not discussed the matter at this moment, how much additional time would that be?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's -- what I did, of course, as Your Honour appreciates, I had a quick run-through of the points with Mr. Krajisnik just to get an indication. There are one or two areas we would need to explore in more detail. It may be that we could cover the ground satisfactorily in about an hour. I say that with some reservation, Your Honour, because after all when it's a question of somebody saying that they spoke to Mr. Krajisnik on a particular occasion - I'm not being so secretive about the content of this, it makes sense to give some broad indication - they spoke to Mr. Krajisnik on a particular occasion, or they met Mr. Krajisnik on a particular occasion, of course that does raise the possibility that in order to be satisfied, because with due respect to Mr. Dubicic, it wouldn't follow necessarily that Mr. Krajisnik might remember everybody that he had met. With no disrespect to Mr. Dubicic, we accept this element of the case that Mr. Krajisnik was a rather more significant figure in Bosnia than Mr. Dubicic. Personal lives. So Mr. Krajisnik may not remember and that may require us to check so that -- so I don't know that that's not an additional difficulty for us. But I would at least hope that we would be able to deal with all or most of the matters and with a bit of luck sufficiently in about one hour. That's best estimate at the moment, Your Honour. That's all I can really say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One of the hesitations, of course, this Chamber might have is that to properly assess the importance of this addition would depend on the information the witness could provide, and since the Defence invited us not to look at it, so we only know that there has been a contact, it could have been a birthday party, it could have been that you meet someone in a shop, shopping at the same time. It could be anything. So therefore, I'm not -- I fully understand the position of the Defence. I don't look into the information. But I think the Defence also should be aware of the handicaps this could cause the Chamber to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I might say straight away - if I may interrupt Your Honour, only to help the Tribunal - is to say that our initial reaction, of course, before we spoke to Mr. Krajisnik at all was to ask the Tribunal not to look at it simply out of a matter of precaution. In fact, I don't take that position now in the light of Your Honour's observation. We would be content for the Tribunal briefly to look at this outline in order to get the feel of it. Because it's more a question really of what lies beyond it that is perhaps the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's a matter, I think, the Chamber should consider, not just by bending to the left and bending to the right. We'll adjourn for, I would say, anything between five and ten minutes. --- Break taken at 11.19 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Looking at the clock, you could say that the Chamber took twice the time it indicated. You also could say that it took only ten minutes more. We have considered the matter. We have looked into the additional information we could expect from this witness if examined on what appears in the supplemental information sheet. The Chamber is not of the opinion that it is irrelevant. Neither is the Chamber of the opinion that it would have no probative value. But for introducing new elements at such a late stage, the threshold should be far higher. Information should be of such a relevance that it would justify this new course to take. Having looked at the information, it would mainly confirm, if that would be the testimony of the witness, that Mr. Krajisnik was aware of what happened in Kravica, which might not be a great surprise, given the attention perhaps these events might have got at that time. But apart from that, it doesn't say much more than that. One even could wonder whether there are not elements in the statement that could be also in favour of the Defence. Therefore, the Chamber has concluded that there's no need and it will not allow the Prosecution to ask additional questions on the issue. If, however, the Defence would like to cross-examine the witness on any of the information contained in this supplemental information sheet, the Defence should indicate so, and under those circumstances, of course, the Prosecution should be allowed to put additional questions on that as well. So it's put in the hands of the Defence whether the information is of such relevance that it would like to elicit more information from the witness on the issue, thus opening the door for the Prosecution to put questions in this respect as well. That's our ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Then we're ready to call, then, our next witness, Mr. Dubicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. And the text of this declaration is now handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Please be seated. Mr. Dubicic, since you have already been interviewed before by investigators of the Prosecution, and since the Chamber has read your statement, your statement will just be summarised so that it's known to the public as well what your statement was about. You'll then not be examined any further by the Prosecution, but you'll be cross-examined by Defence counsel. Mr. Hannis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And if I may make a request, I intended to read out that summary that the Court has. There were four questions I wanted to ask him concerning his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Some brief questions. If it's not entering new grounds and if it's just small clarifications, you're allowed to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. With regard to this witness, the summary is as follows: The witness was born in Bratunac municipality and lived there until he left with the start of the war in April 1992. The population of Bratunac was 33.750, of which about 63 per cent were Bosniaks and 33 per cent were Serbs. In the 1990 elections, the SDA party won 51 per cent of the vote and the SDS got 31 per cent. The executive positions in the municipality were divided evenly, three and three. The witness was chosen president of Bratunac municipality. The local SDS president was Miroslav Deronjic. This witness describes two separate incidents in August 1991 in which he successfully resisted efforts of the army and local Serbs to seize mobilisation records from the municipality and his discussion with Miroslav Deronjic about that. On 3 September 1991, two Bosniaks were killed in the village of Kravica. On 4 September, Radovan Karadzic was on television, saying that no municipal or republican officials were permitted to approach Kravica. Miroslav Deronjic also stated that it was impossible for republic-level inspectors to go to Kravica to investigate. On 5 September 1991, a republic-level delegation, including Nikola Koljevic, came to Bratunac. Only Koljevic was invited to speak to the Serb people in Kravica. Around this time, the witness had information that weapons were being distributed to Serb houses during the night. By April 1992, Miroslav Deronjic had formed a Bratunac SDS Crisis Staff but had relocated it to nearby Ljubovija in Serbia. Some 4.000 to 5.000 soldiers were stationed there. Heavy artillery pointed towards Bratunac, was positioned in the hills above Ljubovija. On 4 April 1992, the Bratunac assembly passed a decision allowing Serbs to create their own police force. Local Serbs began setting up barricades and checkpoints with armed guards in villages such as Kravica and Polom. On 17 April 1992, the witness was advised by the head of the police that there was "some sort of army" inside Bratunac town. Miroslav Deronjic eventually came and told this witness that he, Mr. Dubicic, was to go to the Hotel Fontana for a meeting. The witness, accompanied by local SDA president Dzevad Gusic and two other Muslims went to the hotel. There they saw armed men, paramilitaries from Arkan's and Seselj's units. Miroslav Deronjic pointed out the commander of these troops. This man had a white eagle insignia and the words "Serbian army" on his uniform. The witness later learned that this unit had the name "Slaughterers of Vukovar Battlefield." This commander told the witness that it was his, the commander's, duty to take over the town, because it had been planned that Bratunac would become part of Republika Srpska.
