The commander told the Muslim delegation that if they didn't want to surrender weapons and legal authorities in peace, then he could enter the town with 4.000 soldiers who were waiting in nearby Ljubovija. The witness was asked to call upon the Bosniaks to surrender, and he was to return to the police station at 6.00 p.m. The Serb forces, including about 70 Arkan's and Seselj's men, took over the police station and took control of the town. The witness fled that same day to Kladanj. In the following days, Bratunac was occupied by units from both the Novi Sad and Valjevo Corps. Other Serbs besides Deronjic, who helped the takeover of Bratunac included Dusko Glisic, Rodoljub Djukanovic, Sreten Radic, and Zivko Radic. These latter two men provided money to Arkan's and Seselj's units in Bratunac. Zivko Radic, a car mechanic before the war, was appointed chief of police immediately after the takeover. This witness also heard hearsay reports about the destruction of mosques in the municipality. That concludes my reading of the summary, Your Honours, and the four questions I want to ask him are as follows. Examined by Mr. Hannis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dubicic, were you a member of a political party, and if so, which one?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the Democratic Action Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with regard to the village of Kravica, what was the ethnicity of that village?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: They were 100 per cent Bosnians of the Orthodox faith.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would that be Muslim, Croat, or Serb?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your statement, in discussing the events in Kravica, you talk about a meeting after which the Crisis Staff of Kravica was -- the English word is "dismissed." My question to you, sir, upon reading that, do you mean they simply left after that meeting or were they somehow fired and removed from their positions?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Disbanded, dismissed. They disbanded the meeting and then never met officially again to decide on anything, with the exception of April 1st, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- thank you. And could we hand the witness a copy of his statement in B/C/S. We have one here. And my last question, Mr. Dubicic, relates to paragraph 24 of your statement, which actually, in the English version, Your Honour, begins at the bottom of a page but then carries over to the next page. Do you find that, Mr. Dubicic?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talk about 4th of April, 1992 assembly meeting at which the SDS requested that a decision be passed for the Serbs to create their own police force. And as I understand it, the SDA had a majority in the municipality and could have prevented such a motion, but you agreed to it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell the Judges, please, why you agreed to the Serbs' request to have a separate police force.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: I agreed so that they would be satisfied, so that they don't think that anybody was denying anything to anyone. We behaved in a very democratic way, because they were under the conception that they were being discriminated against and they wanted to form their own police, so we said: "Okay. Form your own police." We wanted to fulfil the requests or the desires of the representatives of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no other questions of this witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Is the Defence ready to cross-examine the witness? Then please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Stewart:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you look, please, at paragraph 3 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: I've looked at paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say there are no JNA barracks in Bratunac municipality, the closest is Mali Zvornik in Serbia. That's about -- correct me if I've got this wrong, but is that about 70 kilometres from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: It is exactly 42 kilometres from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The -- going on to the next paragraph, you say, in the second sentence -- do you see that, paragraph 4, it says: "A year before the multi-party system, we could already feel some political movements in Bratunac, even from TV and radio reports." Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "some political movements," what sort of movements are you talking about there?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: I'm saying that because in that period, in 1990, the Serb population began to move out of Bratunac. Some said that they were allegedly being threatened. So when the whole situation became clear, it was said that the individuals were moving away due to economic reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to date this, you're talking, are you, there, when you say a year before the multi-party system, you're talking are you about a year before the elections of November 1990? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you say -- the English is you say that you could feel those political movements even from television and radio reports. You wouldn't have needed television and radio reports to feel those political movements, as you've described them, would you?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: That information on television was broadcast by Serbian or Belgrade television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. I'll rephrase this, or put the question slightly differently. Are you saying that it was only from television and radio reports that you obtained this information about the movement out of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Since I lived in that region, I also noticed it myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm wondering why you bothered to refer to television and radio reports at all. You don't need those, from what you said, as a source of information. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: When I provided this statement, this is what I was asked, so I gave my answers to the questions that were put to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what were you asked that led to the reference to television and radio reports?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: This was just a confirmation of what was going on, as I stated it, what was going on in the area of the Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to the last couple of sentences in the same paragraph. You were working in Serbia at the time?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Presumably, from your next comment, you had been working in Serbia since at least the mid-1980s; is that correct? When did you first start working in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: On the 22nd of October, 1972.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you refer to the memorandum as you describe it, the memorandum of Greater Serbia, in 1986. So you're going back -- straight away you're going back several years from the first part of paragraph 4 of your statement. That's clear, isn't it? Well, you're talking about 1989 in the first half of that paragraph, and then you go back to 1986.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: I replied to the questions the investigators put to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your last sentence says: "That was the beginning." You refer to the memorandum of Greater Serbia. That was a memorandum produced by a group including some well-known academics, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say that was the beginning of the preparations for the events that followed in the years to come. Do you mean by that that, in your view, it was the beginning of a chain of events rather than some conscious preparation for what happened then in subsequent years?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you now what the memorandum said, then it is certainly the beginning of something that would ensue in the coming period. We weren't even thinking about the possibility that something like that would happen to us in the beginning of 1992. For us, this was an indication that that association was preparing what would happen to us in 1991 and the period after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you may be relieved to know that I'm not going to ask you to tell the Tribunal about the contents of that memorandum or to explore that particular bit of the history with you. We can move on to paragraph 5 of your statement. You say: "Leading up to the 1990 elections." We're talking about the November 1990 elections, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: September. In September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say: "The various parties were established in September 1990. The elections were in November." That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to confirm with you: The two people that you refer to in the middle of that paragraph, Mr. Velibor Ostojic and Mr. Rajko Dukic, Mr. Ostojic became a minister in the power-sharing arrangements between the three nationalities - Croats, Serbs, and Muslims - after the 1990 elections, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Rajko Dukic was the chair of the -- or became the chair of the Executive Board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then going on to paragraph 6 of your statement, towards the end, it's the last few lines, there's a sentence that begins: "The weapons and equipment for Territorial Defence had already been taken away in May 1990 to the Tuzla Corps." Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'm going to again risk a distance, but correct it as you think fit. Tuzla -- well, how far is Tuzla from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: About 100 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Tuzla, of course, is a -- that's a pretty large town, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: It has a population of 60.000, the town of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you go on, the last sentence you say: "There was another police commander elected first." Well, you refer to commander named Milosevic. That's a different Milosevic from the well-known person who is here in The Hague. You say: "There was another Serb police commander elected first. He was from Serbia. His name was Momcilo Mandic."

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Please read it. That's it. Yes. There was a typing mistake. It is Momcilo Milosevic. If you read it to the end, then you will see what the true version is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're saying that in the last line of that paragraph, Momcilo Mandic should read Momcilo Milosevic, are you?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: It says Momcilo Mandic. There is no Milosevic. That was a typing mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The previous sentence -- let's get this clear. The previous sentence, you say: "Chief of police was Nezir Muratovic, and commander of police was named Milosevic. There was another Serb police commander elected first. He was from Serbia. His name was Momcilo Mandic. He was replaced in a later development." Now, the way it reads -- just bear with me for a moment. The way it reads is that first of all, Momcilo Mandic was the police commander; later, it was Mr. Milosevic who was the police commander. Are you saying that that's wrong?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: The police commander at the time was Momcilo Mandic. Milosevic came later, after Mr. Mandic submitted his resignation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is in fact exactly what -- apart from the additional reference, resignation, that's exactly what your statement is saying. Just take a -- I don't want to rush you on this. Just take a moment to read those two sentences carefully, because I suggest that what your statement is saying is exactly what you've just said.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: The chief of police was Nezir Muratovic, and the police commander was Mandic. So there was just a typing mistake. Instead of Mandic, it was written Milosevic. And then in the next sentence, this typing mistake is corrected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry. That is not the way it reads. I'm going to have to just try and clear this up with you. Forget about the chief of police. That's a different position from commander of police, isn't it? Are we agreed on that?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are two different positions: Chief of police and commander of police. Do we agree about that?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: The chief of police is the chief of police, and the commander, I agree, the head of the police is the chief of the police. That is the chief. And the commander is, yes, yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So we can -- for immediate purposes, forget about Mr. Muratovic. We've got two people you mention: Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Mandic. Is it correct that each of those was at some point commander of the police?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: It is correct. Where it says here "Milosevic," actually, Mandic is supposed to be there. When Mandic submitted his resignation, we appointed Milosevic for the -- as police commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Witness, I'm not going to debate with you what your statement means. It's clear what you're saying now. Mandic was first the commander of the police, and then Milosevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say that Mandic was replaced in a later development. What was that development, as you describe it?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic was replaced in September, in early September. I think this was on 5th of September when he was replaced. The events in question are actually the killing of those two Bosniaks in the village of Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you -- in the next sentence -- paragraph, paragraph 7, you refer to the requirement for a majority of votes in the Bratunac municipality. That's the Municipal Assembly you're talking about there, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Could you please ask your question again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in the -- next paragraph 7, the one at the foot of the page you say: "The statute of our municipality had been changed just before the elections. It had been required that only a majority of votes was required to pass decisions, but the Communist Party had changed the requirement to two-thirds of the votes." That relates to the Municipal Assembly, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That was the statute of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then going on -- it's over the page in the English version, but going on a couple of sentences, do you see a sentence beginning: "Even though we had the majority and could have changed the statute again." Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, "we" means the Muslim community; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: The organs of authority of the municipality, as well as the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're agreeing with what I've just put to you, are you, that "we" means the Muslim community? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Well, let's say it's that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's not say it unless it's true. You're giving evidence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you say "we had the majority," it looks as if you mean the two-thirds majority. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: No, we did not have the two-thirds majority. We had more than a half, and that was true until 1990, when the status of the municipality changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, please explain then, how you could have changed the statute again if a two-thirds majority was required and you didn't have a two-thirds majority.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: We accepted this statute from 1990, and we didn't change it. But according to the rules, we were able to change it because the statute that was valid until 1990, only a simple majority was required. We did not need a two-thirds majority. In principle, we wanted to take decisions in the municipality, or in the Municipal Assembly, by general agreement. We didn't want the citizenship to be divided along ethnic or other lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You make that point. But let me be more specific. When did the Communist Party change the requirement to two-thirds of the votes?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: It changed the requirement in 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What month? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: I really couldn't say which month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, all right. Was it the first half of 1990 or the second half of 1990?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: I think it was in the first half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the position was that a two-thirds majority was required under that statute, but you, the Muslim community, didn't have a two-thirds majority; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to paragraph 8 of your statement, where you refer to a big incident that took place. Your words: Big incident that took place in the middle of August 1991, when the army units arrived. And then you say -- well, they came on two occasions in Tuzla to take away the mobilisation records: "We didn't give the records to them and they had to leave without them." The "we" in that sentence means who?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: The organs of the Bratunac municipality, the authorities, that is, and the Bosniaks who lived in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you involved in that decision or result that they had to leave without those records, you personally?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: I was involved, because I was between the army and the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what sense were you between them?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: When they came, they got off the lorries and they started toward the municipal building, and there were Bosniaks outside the municipal building. And they started firing immediately. Volleys of gunfire started. They probably had orders to that effect. I was in the centre of these events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We may be talking about two different dates. You start off talking about the army units coming on two occasions in the second half of August and going away without the records, but that's before the incident and event of the 31st of August, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you were going on to describe was that incident, wasn't it, the 31st of August?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the two earlier occasions, they had -- the army units had arrived from Tuzla and they had come and gone peacefully, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: That's correct. They came and they were very civil when they talked to me. I showed them the order that I had from the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which said that I should not give up the military documentation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the -- what at that time was the population of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: How do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people lived in Bratunac at that time?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: At that time, the population of Bratunac was 32.750.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's nicely precise. Thank you. And at that time - we're talking about August 1991 - had there already been a significant departure of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: From time to time, Serbs would leave, probably because they were talked into it, and they left for the neighbouring municipality, Ljubovija, but they didn't move far away from us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that the SDS had organised their members in front of the municipal building. What do you -- can you say what level of membership you remember the SDS having at that time in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: I don't know the number of the membership, but I know how many citizens we had of Christian Orthodox faith.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many was it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's a bit more than the -- not a lot, but a bit more than the 33 per cent which you give in your statement as the Serb element of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: What I just said is true. When the elections were completed and when the election results were published, those are the results we got.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I just ask you: I don't know whether it's so important to know whether it's 33 or 34 per cent, but if you refer to his statement, you certainly have noticed where he gave the number in his testimony today, it was a thousand lower than he gave in his statement. In the statement it's 33.750, and that makes 11.200 a little bit under one-third. Perhaps I should have refrained from this observation, but perhaps, as long as the difference is not more than two, three, or five per cent, and if it's not really of great relevance, we could go over the matter perhaps a bit more quickly. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, that cleared up a point I was just about to clear up, because it's plain that it's very near to the 33 per cent anyway. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But turning to something else, you say: "I think there were several thousand of those Serbs in front of the municipal building. They blocked the building." Is it -- a large gathering is a large gathering, but are you able to be a little bit more specific about "several thousand"?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: I could say there were four or five thousand citizens of Christian Orthodox faith.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That must have been, given the -- well, given that a lot of the population are going to be children, so on that figure that's getting on for something quite close to the entire male adult population, isn't it, of Serbs in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Not only the male population. There were ladies there as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say in that paragraph, towards the end, you say you knew that the SDS leaders were aware that the army was coming, "When I had driven over the river I saw some of the SDS leaders talking to the army officers." Well, it follows, of course you and your colleagues knew the army was coming as well, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of it. It was Friday, the 31st of August, 1991. However, people had gathered, and I told the SDS president after that meeting that it was them who organised it. I asked him: "Who told these people to assemble?" And he said: "I don't know. They did so spontaneously." And I told him that the police had arrived and they were about to cross the bridge into Bosnia, and I had seen SDS representatives with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on to the next paragraph, paragraph 9. You say the situation was now very dangerous. There was also a large crowd of Bosniaks gathered in the square. So how many Bosniaks were there?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Well, there must have been three to four thousand, not less, because Friday is the day when Muslims go to the mosque. That day they didn't go to the mosque. Instead they all assembled there, and word must have spread, and even great numbers came. Two crowds gathered, Muslims -- Bosniaks of Muslim faith and Muslim -- and Bosniaks of Orthodox faith, and between these two large crowds, there was I.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the army commander who you refer to in that paragraph, a captain who approached and told you that you would be responsible for all tragic events which would happen from then on, what was his name?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: That captain didn't tell me his name. I just told him that it was not polite to come that way. He should have announced his visit and come to my office. I didn't like the way he was talking to me, and I had the impression that he was threatening me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I get this clear, then: There was this major event in Bratunac involving thousands of Bosniaks who were Muslims, thousands of Serbs, the military presence, you have an hour and a half discussion with this army commander, the captain, and you didn't know then, and you still don't know now, his name? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You weren't sufficiently curious even to ask somebody else who he was if you didn't know?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Those who knew certainly wouldn't have told me, and I couldn't ask him, nor could I approach those soldiers, because they were not regular troops. They were older soldiers, donning beards and they must have been from the Territorial Defence or some paramilitary unit had arrived from outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suggest to you that's a bit unreal. The idea that you couldn't simply ask the commander that was talking to you for an hour and a half what his name was. He wouldn't have refused to tell you who he was, would he?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: All this took place in the street, outside the town hall, outside the municipal building. So it was not a normal conversation. We were trying to outtalk each other. We were arguing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us any clue to his identity, since you don't apparently know his name?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you anything about his identity, because, truth to tell, I know nothing about him. I didn't make inquiries later either. I tried to inquire about him in the corps in Tuzla, but they couldn't tell me anything about the incident involving the arrival of those troops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you tried to inquire about him subsequently, did you?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes, later, when I went to visit the corps for some other reason, because I had some troops in one of the local communes and I asked them on that occasion who those soldiers could have been, and they didn't tell me anything. They couldn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But can we summarise what happened accurately this way. Confirm if this is right. There was a dangerous situation with two very large crowds of Muslims and Serbs, both present; that nobody was injured on that occasion; and that after a lengthy discussion between you and the commander, they did leave with part of the -- well, no. They left without what they came for. That's correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Dusk came. They picked up and left without the documentation, after the argument we had. They wanted to collect the documents at least for the Serb conscripts, but I refused to give them that too, because I was president of the entire municipality, including all the citizens, and I was required to respect the decision of the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which said that I should not give up the military documentation to the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the army -- they didn't achieve what they came for in terms of getting the records, but they did achieve one perfectly normal and acceptable aim for an army, but nobody was hurt in the whole day? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Nobody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to paragraph 12. And you refer here to the commander of police forces, Momcilo Mandic. You say: "He wasn't available in town," by which you mean obviously in Bratunac. You say he was supposed to be in the MUP building. When you say supposed to be in the MUP building, do we take it you don't actually mean any more than that that was his normal headquarters and that was his base where he worked?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: I ordered the MUP that in that period the commander of the police and the head of the MUP should take turns and be on duty every night at the police station. That night, when I said he wasn't there, he was supposed to be at the police station, according to the roster. This schedule was in force only during that period when these problems were a regular occurrence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't he in fact supposed to be where, in his judgement, he was most required to be in the exercise of his duties?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was supposed to be at the police station, because that's his first and foremost responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next paragraph. The next day, 4th of September, you say: "Avdo Hebib arrived in Bratunac with Vitomir Zepinic, along with some inspectors, Enver Halvadzija ..." Which of those gentlemen mentioned there, Avdo Hebib, Vitomir Zepinic and Enver Halvadzija, which of those are Muslims?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Avdo Hebib is a Muslim, whereas Mr. Zepinic is of Christian Orthodox faith.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Enver, he was a Muslim as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Enver Halvadzija is also a Muslim. And there were also two other investigators. Enver Dupovac and Mr. Skondric, the first being a Muslim and the latter a Serb, a leader of the investigation team from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And similarly, if we go on to paragraph 16, where you say we appointed an inspector from Tuzla MUP Emin Kaknjasevic. Was he a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the next paragraph, 17, you say: "The delegation from Sarajevo returned there and the situation was still very tense. Bosniaks were frightened and the Serbs were still gone. During the night we received information that some Chetnik units were approaching. Fortunately it wasn't true." But where did that information come from?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Since I spent all my time at the MUP during that period, from the 3rd onwards, I can say that we received that information over the telephone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From -- that's how. From whom?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: The caller who gave us this warning did not identify himself. He just said what he had to say and hung up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as you say it was wrong anyway, the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, it's 20 minutes to 1.00. We have to have another break. Could you give us an indication on how much time you'd still need for your cross-examination? Because we also have to reserve time for short oral argument on the issue we dealt with yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I would think I would probably complete my cross-examination, apart from unexpected turns in the evidence, within half an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's then have a break for 15 minutes, that is, until 5 minutes to 1.00. If you could then finish in half an hour and avoid whatever is unexpected.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that's not entirely in my hands, Your Honour, but I will do my best on that, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You understand that this is my sense of humour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It was appreciated, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then we have 20 minutes left for argument, oral argument on the issues still outstanding. We adjourn until 5 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's a couple of points that arise out of what you were saying before the break. Is this correct, that at that time, strictly speaking, as a legal and organisational matter, such matters as military documentation of the type that was being sought from you on those visits, the mobilisation records, was under the competence of the republic Territorial Defence staff and not strictly the Bosnia and Herzegovina presidency?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: I received an order from the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I didn't receive any kind of written notification from the military structures of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the answer that you don't know the answer to my question?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: I know the answer to your question in one -- in a republic, the civilian top organ is the one that is responsible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put it another way, then. Was the normal position that such matters as military -- control of military documentation and provision of mobilisation records were normally at that time under the competence and authority of the republic Territorial Defence staff?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: In a given situation, when they asked for some exercises to be organised, and there were such exercises, on a couple of occasions, upon orders of the military structures, we carried out the mobilisation of people, and that was under their jurisdiction. But I repeat again: Here, in this case, during the first and the second visit, they were probably informed. They didn't receive any documentation. They didn't call us. They didn't contact us in any way to order us to do it and in any different way than we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you contact them?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: I did not get in contact with the military structures in reference to providing this documentation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you about something else, then. Do you agree it's correct that you, as the president of the Municipal Assembly, strictly speaking, didn't have the legal authority over the MUP?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: The MUP was directly subordinated to the republican Ministry for Internal Affairs, but naturally, we consulted each other. We proposed new leaders and also if any new -- any police posts needed to be filled after somebody retired or in accordance with the population structure, there was a certain number of police officers that was required for a certain percentage of the population. But there were some other things also that were agreed upon with the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go back to your statement, please, to paragraph 19 -- I'm sorry, paragraph 17. This relates to the delegation that arrived in a helicopter. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say: "While we talked --" you spoke to them. You asked what you were supposed to do, and then: "While we talked," you say, "a person entered the office and told Mr. Koljevic that the Serb people expected him to come to Kravica." Can you say who that person was?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the name. I don't know the name. But I know the person is from Kravica, because I used to go there for meetings, often for various reasons, and Mr. Koljevic stood up right away and I said that he could not go by himself because I was the president of the municipality and the president of all the citizens in the municipality of Bratunac. And then he decisively told me that: "You should not go. You cannot go with me. The things that I have to say to them, I cannot say in front of you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going on a couple of paragraphs, paragraph 19, the next day Hebib returned to Bratunac with Mr. Ostojic and other politicians, and then you refer to Mr. Karadzic. And you say: "When the latest delegation arrived I contacted the Kravica Serb Crisis Staff by telephone." Is this correct that at that time, and we're talking about September 1991, the idea of crisis staffs was part of the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: They were not part of the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I beg your pardon. My mistake. Part of the constitution of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: They were not a part of the Yugoslav constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it -- at that time was it perfectly normal to have -- well, normal at that time, in that situation, that you would find in some places a Serb crisis staff, in some places you would find a Muslim crisis staff, and in some places you would find both?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: In the region of Bratunac municipality, our municipality occasionally there would be both crisis staff, and I'm speaking responsibly. I'm telling the truth. And that is that the Muslim crisis staffs or Bosniak crisis staffs were much, much rarer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- you say in paragraph 21 -- I beg your pardon, let's take paragraph 20 first. The investigation team, you refer to the disbanding of the Kravica Crisis Staff, as you put it in your evidence earlier today. Then you go on: "The investigation team did find out who were the murderers. One was from Kravica. The other was from Ljubovija." Do you know their names?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: I knew their names, but I've forgotten them. This is before, when I was providing a statement in 1999. So this was ten years ago. The truth is that one of them was from the municipality of Ljubovija, and the other one was an inhabitant from Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying you had already forgotten their names by the time you gave the statement in 1999?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Nobody asked me for their names in 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can't remember their names, which you say, can you remember anything about them?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: This citizen from Kravica was a driver by profession. They were between 30 and 40 years old, the two of them. This person from the Ljubovija region, he had some kind of shop in one of the local communes of the municipality of Ljubovija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was the murder done, as far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: There was an ambush set up, and those two citizens who were killed were not supposed to be killed. They just happened to be in the car. This person who was actually driving the vehicle, he had some kind of disagreement with the citizens of Kravica, so they probably intended to kill him. They fired from firearms from the ambush, and these two just happened to be killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were the wrong people altogether? I'm not saying there are right people to kill, but these were the wrong people, as far as the murderers were concerned? They got the wrong people; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: They got the wrong people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then paragraph 21, you say: "We had information that weapons were being distributed. We heard that Serb houses during the night were to leave the lights completely off," and so on. "We" again is the Muslim leadership in Bratunac at the time; is that what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: I am talking on behalf the political workers of the municipality of Bratunac. That's what I was informed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did your information come from?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: The information came from a couple of citizens who received such weapons during the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were Serbs, were they?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes. But they were honest people who reported back to me. All of them talked to me. They were probably bothered by the fact that they were given this. They said nothing we said is made up. There was a mistake. One of the weapons was left at a house of one of the Bosniaks by mistake that night also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the source of the information, then? The Bosniak whose doorstep the weapon was left on, or a Serb?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: The initial information came from Serb citizens of the Christian Orthodox faith.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we move on to paragraph 30. You refer to the commander. If you need to read just the end of the previous paragraph to refresh your mind about that sentence, please do.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: You can continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was the commander?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: The commander was -- he had the insignia on the left hand, the insignia of the Serb army. He had a beard. It was a gentleman in his 40s. I could not ask for their ID. They did not introduce themselves to me. They did not say who they were. And when there was a meeting and when the question was put - "Who is this army?" - there was no answer. They said they didn't know. I responded only to questions that were asked of me. How could I have asked who he was when there was a person holding a gun to my forehead as they were talking?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was holding a gun to your forehead?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: One of the persons who was escorting him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't say anything when you gave this statement about somebody holding a gun to your head because nobody asked you whether somebody was holding a gun to your head; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is getting a little unreal, isn't it? How far would you have carried your non-response to anything except a question? If people have been slaughtered in front of your eyes would you not have mentioned it because you hadn't been asked?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I would have mentioned it. Perhaps I would have mentioned something like that, had something like that happened. Thank God, they didn't fire at my forehead, but the truth is that they did hold a gun to my head. This is something that happened to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I suggest to you that that's simply an embellishment and that it's just ludicrous to suppose that in describing this incident to the investigators you wouldn't have made it clear to them what the tone of that meeting was by somebody having held a gun to your head.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Nothing here is embellished. I repeat, I repeat: When I was providing the statement, I tried to tell only the truth. When I was providing the statements, I was keeping the truth in mind and then I talked. As far as what I didn't say regarding this gun, nothing happened to me and I didn't mention it. It's true that nobody asked me and I didn't -- it didn't occur to me at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the funny thing is that you say in your statement that you told him: "We could not negotiate under threat, that the Serb population was not in danger, we didn't have weapons, there's no need for Serbs to be frightened." So you apparently had the guts with a gun being pointed at your head to tell him you couldn't negotiate under threat but couldn't bring yourself to be brave enough to ask his name. Is that an accurate summary of the position?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I decided to tell them what you just said, that the Serb people were not under threat, and I even addressed the president of the SDS municipal board to tell him that, but he didn't say a word. I had to say that, even if the price for saying that would have been my life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say: "I knew that Bosniaks had no weapons." How sweeping do you mean that? Do you mean that as far as you were concerned, no Bosniaks had any weapons?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes. No Bosniak had weapons. Yes. Except for hunting rifles. But this is a sports weapon, and those who had such weapons also had a licence for them. But if we're talking about Kalashnikovs or other kinds of rifles, none of them had anything like that for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your statement said, "I knew that Bosniaks had no weapons," not "no Kalashnikovs," doesn't it? Agreed?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not just Kalashnikovs. They did not have weapons to wage war with. That's the weapon that I meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next paragraph, 31, you refer to your getting out to Kladanj. How did you get out, get to Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: I went to Konjevic Polje. I fled through the woods and then from Konjevic Polje, I was taken to Kladanj with a vehicle, some person, a man took me to Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who helped you?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Nobody helped me. I decided to do that myself. I felt that my presence there was pointless. There was nobody to talk with about anything. During this meeting when we were talking, I was ordered to be at the police station at 6.00. This was on the 17th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the vehicle that you referred to, did you arrange that yourself?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: I didn't arrange it. Just a vehicle drove up and I stopped it, got in, and I left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, I see. So when you say you fled through the woods and then you were taken to Kladanj with a vehicle, it was -- you just waved down or stopped a vehicle in the road, did you?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: That's correct. When I came to the crossroads at Konjevic Polje, on the road that leads to Konjevic Polje, I stopped there and I was trying to stop two or three vehicles. One of them stopped. I got into the vehicle and went to Kladanj in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let's be clear. So there was no organised help at all. You simply went entirely on your own. You stopped this vehicle that you didn't know before and you were taken to where you wanted to go. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next paragraph, 32, you talk about two rich Serbs, Mr. Radic -- well, Mr. Radic and Mr. Radic, two different Mr. Radics, provided money to bring Arkan's and Seselj's units to Bratunac. Do you have any firsthand knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: When I called Bratunac from Tuzla, I called some citizens of Serb ethnicity, since they were the only ones there, and that's when I got this information. I was told that - I think this was in May 1992 - that they came and asked for money, that they even organised some kind of protest in front of the municipal building in Bratunac, and that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Who organised some sort of protest?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Arkan's and Seselj's men, the people who came to Bratunac in order to create unrest, so that the army could come in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The way you describe it, you say: "I learned there was a meeting in the square and these units asked for the two rich Serbs by name, asking for their money." Is what you're saying that there was some sort of shouting out of their name by a group or a crowd?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: I wasn't told that, but I did ask who was it who was supposed to give money, and that's the answer I got, and their names were mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just asking you -- you say: "These units asked for the two rich Serbs by name." I'm just asking you to clarify. If you don't know, you don't know, but to clarify who did they ask, and how?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Well, they asked for the money that had been promised, and they know who had promised them the money if they come. I didn't mention it because I know. But out of the crowd, they called out those two people that I named, and that's the information I got. I got those two names.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just two short items. Re-examined by Mr. Hannis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dubicic, you mentioned a Momcilo Mandic who was commander of the police in your municipality. Do you know another Momcilo Mandic who later became the minister of justice in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: I know. I know. He worked in the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is the Momcilo Mandic I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is the police commander that you've been talking about in Bratunac a different person than the one who was later minister of justice in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's a different person. He used to be a teacher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The only other item, Your Honour, refers to -- I think it's at line 11, page 61 in the transcript. When you were talking about -- it's not in your written statement, sir. But when we were talking about the incident when the army came to try and seize the mobilisation records, you talked about the crowd consisting of Bosniaks of Muslim faith, and then you also mentioned Bosniaks of Orthodox faith. And I don't know if you're using the term "Bosniak" generally or if you meant to say Serbs of Orthodox faith. Can you clear that up for me, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interfere at this moment? Before we get an explanation, I'd first like to ask the witness whether there's not a misunderstanding. Did you mean to say Bosnians of the one religion and Bosnians of the other religion? Is that what you meant to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. Bosnians. Generally speaking, I'm trying to avoid calling people Muslims or Serbs. I'm trying to stick to the term "Bosnians," of either Muslim, Orthodox or Catholic faith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I interrupted you because that's a mistake in the transcript. Bosnians has been by mistake written down as Bosniaks. I noticed already that the witness very much insisted on using Bosnian and then mentioned the faith to which these Bosnians belonged.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I had, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you'd allow me, just a word. Bosnia would be a happy state if it had more Bosnians who didn't insist on any faith, who would be happy to call themselves simply Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's how I felt you wanted to express yourself. Judge El Mahdi has one or more questions for you. JUDGE EL MAHDI: Thank you, Mr. President. Questioned by the Court: JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Witness, I would like a clarification of one point. In your statement, you said, and I'm quoting in English, it is referring to the day after your departure. [In English] "The following days, Bratunac was occupied by units from Novi Sad Corps and Valjevo Corps. They then started with tortures." [Interpretation] I understand that when you say "they," you mean the Novi Sad Corps and the Valjevo Corps. In the following paragraph, you said, and I quote again: [In English] "On 19 May 1992, Arkan's and Seselj's troops returned and asked for their promised money." [Interpretation] So my question is: What you heard, because at the moment when all this was happening, that was all after your departure, was it the Novi Sad Corps and the Valjevo Corps -- my first question is, actually: To what army to these corps belong? And my second question is: You attribute the events that followed, that is, the murders and the expulsions, to those troops. Do you attribute those events to them, to the Novi Sad and Valjevo Corps, or you attribute them to Arkan and other paramilitary units? Would you like to answer this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there a technical problem? It seems that Mr. Dubicic doesn't hear anything. That's the unexpected. Is it a matter of choosing the channel or ... Mr. Dubicic, can you now hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge El Mahdi, you have to repeat the question. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Witness, I would like to ask you the following question: When you say that the following day after your departure, the troops that you call Novi Sad and Valjevo Corps, to what army do these troops belong? Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you. Yes. Those troops, the Novi Sad Corps and the Valjevo Corps, were probably regular troops, but there must have been among them people who were mobilised, conscripts who had been doing their regular military service before. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes, but you said in your statement, and I'm quoting: [In English], "Then started with tortures, murders, and expulsions."

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] In the following paragraph, though, you say that a certain Arkan and another unit had their troops, which returned to Bratunac to get the money that had been promised them. Is it they that you accuse of those murders, tortures, expulsions, or is it the troops of the Novi Sad and Valjevo Corps?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ DUBICIC
utterances.text: Arkan's men and Seselj's men, while they were in Bratunac, carried out this genocide, but they had come, in my opinion, with the objective to justify the entry of the regular army from Ljubovija. The army troops that had been stationed in Ljubovija seven or eight days prior to the invasion, and they had their guns pointed at Bratunac. They had their artillery trained at Bratunac. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any issue raised by the Bench which would cause additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: None from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Nor from the Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dubicic, that means that this concludes your testimony in this Court. You've answered the questions of all the parties and questions put to you by the Bench. It's important for this Court to hear the testimony of witnesses that have been present at the time when the events happened. I'd like to thank you very much for having come to The Hague, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, you may escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have ten minutes left. We have received the written submissions of the parties in respect of how appropriate it is to hear a witness who is still awaiting to be sentenced under a plea agreement. Before I give a short opportunity to the parties to briefly add what they have to add, I'd like to ask two questions to start with. First of all, in view of the relevant case-law, transparency is one of the first things that would be required at all if deciding whether you could hear a witness, yes or no. Would the Prosecution be ready to provide the Chamber with a copy of the plea agreement, which I take it has been made public under Rule -- well, I've forgotten the Rule, but normally --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no problem in providing that to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's my first question. The second question to the Prosecution is the following: From the summary of the witness statement attached to your response, it does not appear that the Prosecution intends to examine the witness on any direct contacts with Mr. Krajisnik. Is that an impression which is correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, frankly, I'm not 100 per cent certain, but it's my belief that he had no direct contact with Mr. Krajisnik; contacts with Mr. Karadzic, but not Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At least I do not see his name appear. So I take it, then, that we do not get supplementary information sheets which would go in that direction. This is just for the Chamber's information. Then, since the Prosecution has -- the Defence has submitted the motion, is there anything you'd like to add at this moment, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Very briefly. First of all, by way of explanation, but I won't take but a moment on this. It's suggested - I don't think it was an especially tendentious comment in the Prosecution's response - that we had cited incompletely from a judgement and from a textbook. In fact what we had done, as I think Your Honours will be able to see, we had taken out paragraphs which appeared to us to have no direct bearing at all on this particular issue and as far as the passage on evidence was concerned from Judge May's textbook, where he cites a case, we had simply taken the passage which was highlighted in the textbook. So certainly there wasn't -- our attempt was to hone it down to strict relevance rather than to be selective in any way which could confuse. The point that we wish to stress is this: That when, for example, in the case of an accomplice, in a number of jurisdictions, this would include the United Kingdom, the tendency now from the point of view of sentencing, and sentencing policy, is to wait until the end of the case so that the person who remains on trial is sentenced at the same time as an accomplice who, for example, has already pleaded guilty. And that's because it appears, and Your Honours can see, I think, from the material before the Court, there's been a change of approach, and that aspect of sentencing policy is regarded as sufficiently important to, if you like, in many cases, though it's a matter of discretion, to override what might be the conflicting principle, that so far as possible when somebody gives evidence they should have any incentive or inducement to tailor their evidence by reference to any future sentencing removed. But that's where you have a conflict, and the conflict is coming down in the modern jurisprudence in the United Kingdom, for example, in favour of deferral so the Court can look in the round at everybody's participation in the relevant events and achieve the right sentence. We don't have that conflict in this case. Mr. Deronjic, after all, is not indicted in this particular case. What we have in the present instance is we have a witness who is a very important witness, and without going into any of it, that's the Prosecution's position, that he is a very important witness, because he's not just Bratunac; he's brought in under the heading of Bratunac, but he's general and Bratunac and he's general in very significant ways. What we have in the present case is the clear danger of an inducement and an influence on Mr. Deronjic's evidence from the fact that he is not to be sentenced for, I think it's not a fixed time, but I think it's contemplated as being something like a couple of months. But there's no, if you like, there's no countervailing problem about sentencing policy in relation to this case, because it's not this particular Chamber which is sentencing him. So that our position is, quite simply, that since it is possible for that inducement and incentive for Mr. Deronjic to approach his evidence favourably to the Prosecution, a danger which, after all, as a matter of common sense the courts do recognise. Because it is obvious common sense and that's recognised throughout all jurisdictions for practical purposes. It is possible to remove that incentive in the present case simply by his giving evidence at a later date after he's been sentenced. That should be done, because there is, apart from, we'd say, relatively minor matters in the scale of things, matters of practical convenience, there is every reason why that should happen. And whether a reference is in the authorities before the Tribunal, and we cite some passages from some observations of Judge Hunt, to -- concern for the Prosecution's position that they shouldn't expose their witness unnecessarily to criticism or attack on the basis that there is an incentive. It's inherent in that that there is in fact a danger overall and there is a danger for the Defence in having a witness, despite the fact we may comment on that, the much more satisfactory result is not the Tribunal is left having to resolve, and the parties are left having to make their submissions on how far that might or might not have influenced the evidence. The much more satisfactory outcome in those circumstances is to take away the incentive, and that is done very simply in the present case by Mr. Deronjic's evidence here being deferred until after he has been finally sentenced. And that in effect, of course it takes him out of the run of Bratunac witnesses, but if you like that's not his primary place anyway in this case. The real importance of his evidence, because we've got other witnesses in relation to specific Bratunac events, the real thrust of Mr. Deronjic's evidence in this case, and his importance, is the fact that he has evidence, if you like, at a higher level than Bratunac in relation to other events. So that's the simple proposition, Your Honours, that the difficulty and the danger is simply easily solved by ensuring that Mr. Deronjic has been finally sentenced before he gives evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis, or Mr. Gaynor. Is there any additional point?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We understand the Defence concern. However, we think it's not a matter that this Trial Chamber cannot deal with. The incentive that Mr. Deronjic may have with regard to his pending sentencing is something that this Court can take into account. Defence counsel will certainly cross-examine him about that, as well as Your Honours, if you feel more questions are necessary. We think that he -- that is just one of the factors that you will need to take into account in deciding what weight to give his evidence and how much credibility to give to him in his testimony. And you really won't be able to make the final decision about that until the end of this case, when you've heard all the other evidence in this case, from all the witnesses and all the documents and everything else, because there will be, I believe, other evidence that will substantiate or corroborate much of what he says. It's a matter of timing, Your Honour, but we think that the danger is not that great that professional judges can't factor that in appropriately and deal with the danger that the Defence is concerned about. I did have one other matter I wanted to mention, Your Honour. I have some additional authority that we wanted to provide to the Court, and it deals with mainly the practice in England and Wales, the jurisdictions cited most by the Defence. The first is an excerpt from Judge May's on evidence. The 4th edition from 1999, in particular --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Chamber, of course, if you refer to that and say what pages these are, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying it's under my cushion in my bed, but it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's at page 444, Your Honour, the last paragraph on that page. I'm not going to read it all out now, in the interests of time. The second item is a decision from the Court of Appeal in the -- in England and Wales, in a case called Harry Palmer, and we would refer you to page 85 of that handout. The next to the last paragraph, which comments on the cases of Pipe and Payne, which are referred to in the defendant's motion at page 5, and at footnote 14 on page 7. Further on page 86, the second paragraph of that case, we would ask you to take a look at. And finally, the third item is a case from -- a case called Chan, C-H-A-N, from the Privy Council, and we would refer you to page 6 of that decision, the second full paragraph that discusses how these two lines of authority on dealing with cooperating witnesses or accomplices' testimony should be handled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that that's the same decision as the decision referred to in the -- what's the other one? You did not provide us with a copy, but -- the Regina v. Reed. That's references made to -- not only to European Court of Human Rights law but also to domestic law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe that's a different decision, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm asking whether that's the same decision as referred to in Regina v. Reed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then would there be -- is there any further matter to be raised at this moment? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do we have the opportunity, Your Honour, of commenting briefly on the submission made in relation to this authority, which wouldn't take more than about a minute or two?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. A minute or two. And you're talking about the last authority?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I was actually going to do it by reference to the Privy Council authority at page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's at the very end of the large paragraph in the middle, the paragraph being the one in the middle, how should those two lines of authority be drawn together. Just the last four or five lines where it says: "Once the courts have taken the large step, as they undoubtedly have, of recognising that circumstances may justify the calling of a witness who stands to gain by giving false evidence."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down because you're reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm asked to slow down. I'll perhaps read it again more slowly; it's a short passage. "Once the courts have taken the large step, as they undoubtedly have, of recognising that circumstances may justify the calling of a witness who stands to gain by giving false evidence, it becomes impossible to say that what happened in the present case was necessarily contrary to the proper conduct of the murder trial." This is a recognition and we stress this, that it is in fact a large step. Then, because it is a large step in every case as a matter of discretion, one has to look at what the reason is against avoiding that large step. And in the present case, as we've indicated to Your Honours, notwithstanding that, of course, Your Honours are professional Judges, so there is nowhere near precisely the problem there is with a jury, the removal of this difficulty is as we've stressed not a difficult thing to do. There is, in effect, apart from the time at which Mr. Deronjic gives his evidence, there is no factor and no consideration which prevents the Court from removing that inducement. It remains a large step, whatever the reasons, to allow an important witness to give evidence when he has this inducement there in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Two things, Your Honour. I'm advised by e-mail that we do intend to lead some evidence regarding Mr. Deronjic's direct dealings with Mr. Krajisnik. So there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it does not appear in the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that. And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Defence aware of -- I mean, is there anything in the statements that have been disclosed to the Defence about direct contacts? Because if you provide us with a summary, we expect that summary to reflect the important parts of the evidence, and I couldn't say that direct contacts between Mr. Deronjic and Mr. Krajisnik would not be considered as having quite some relevance. So it really surprises me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know the nature of that, and I'm just advising the Court that I didn't want to mislead you with what I said before. It appears that there is some information contrary to what I may have indicated initially. I will check with Mr. Harmon, who will be leading Mr. Deronjic, and see if there should be some supplemental 65 ter or something additional to reflect what it sounds like is being referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know, under these circumstances, whether the Chamber really wanted to give a decision as soon as possible in order not to unnecessarily cause the examination not to start by tomorrow, that we really have to consider this, and we will inform you later this afternoon on two questions: First of all, whether we take a decision this afternoon; and the second, if we take a decision, what that decision then is. Apart from whether we might issue a decision given in oral form later in writing as well, but we have to consider this, and it will not be until the second part of this afternoon that you'll be aware of what the position of the Chamber is. And I also add that you should prepare for all situations, that is, that we start with Mr. Deronjic tomorrow or that we start with Mr. Deronjic later tomorrow morning, or that we do not start with the examination of Mr. Deronjic. But I take it that the Prosecution is able to deal with that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have -- other than Mr. Deronjic, I think the only two remaining witnesses for this portion of the trial are Pat Treanor, our expert, and Mr. Hasanovic, who was a witness that we had difficulties with, it caused a change in the schedule earlier in the week. He may not be able to be here until the 18th. So Mr. Treanor, I think, is the only other witness available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And would there be a possibility for you to start with Mr. Treanor by tomorrow, if for whatever reason I would like not to start with Mr. Deronjic or postpone his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think all things are possible. If Mr. Tieger is watching, I hope he takes note of this conversation and adjusts accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the last thing I have to do is to apologise to the interpreters that I -- and the technicians that I did not ask the permission to steal the last seven minutes of their time. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, same courtroom.
